utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. The apologies of the Chamber for arriving late. We actually received a message that the witness was delayed, and so we've been waiting in our Chambers. But the message turned out to be mistaken. Good morning, sir. Would you please take the card that's given to you now and read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. May I just deal with the witness situation this morning. When the message was passed through to the Bench, the witness was not here and there was no interpreter here either. I thought it appropriate to pass the message through so that the Bench wouldn't come and be inconvenienced. My apologies if I've miscalculated slightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for taking precautions. Fortunately they proved unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I now deal with the following witness, who is a protected witness, 007. Could the witness please be shown a confidential document and indicate whether the names, details, and date of birth included are his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My understanding is that this witness has a pseudonym and facial distortion, but no voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 183, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, may we deal, please, with the evidence that you have some to give. I want to deal with some preliminary matters. Is it right - and I can show you the document if you need to see it - that you completed an official report for the Republic of Croatia, the Ministry of the Interior. That was dated the 15th of May in 1992. Do you remember compiling that report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I do. I didn't actually write the report myself. I provided a verbal account to a police officer who took it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. That was some six months after the event at which you're going to give evidence. Secondly, it's right, is it not, that you then compiled a report for the Office of the Prosecutor for this institution. That was dated the 19th of June, 1995. That's right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That you have given evidence is what is called the Dokmanovic trial. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you have additionally given evidence at the Belgrade inquiry or trial, which was the 24th of May of this year. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just to assist the Court, my learned friends, I believe the date that this witness gave evidence in the Dokmanovic trial was the 3rd of February of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to, if I may, please, firstly refer to the date 1991, and I think at that time you were in Vukovar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just go into private session for a moment to clarify one matter, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you do a military service at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it right - and I think it was in 1966 - you had to serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what part of the JNA did you serve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I was with the infantry in Vrsac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long was your military service for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: One year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal then, please, with the fact - I think you are a married man - that you had two children. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I unfortunately with deal with one of those children in due course. And it's right, as you say, that you lived I believe in the centre of Vukovar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes. Plumb in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to deal in general terms, if I may, with August 1991 and what was occurring in Vukovar itself. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you in very general terms what happened towards the end of August, how matters developed - I will use the word - militarily.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: After May when the police officers in Borovo Selo had been killed, the barricades were still there on all the roads leading to predominantly Serb villages. You couldn't drive there or back. In the first days of August, the first shells landed on the centre of Vukovar, the centre of town, just in front of my house -- or rather, between my house and a department store known as Zagrebacka Nama. That was when the whole thing began.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the actual firing itself, did it continue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: It began with those two shells and then it continued throughout the remaining months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, please -- you say that you were in the centre of Vukovar at that time. Did you see, if we deal perhaps just with August and September for the moment, where many of those shells landed, general locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: The very centre of town and also the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If I deal with what could be called the fall of shot or the fall of the shells, from what you could see were they being targeted on military targets or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you explain to the Court why you say that? Can you give us a picture, please, of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: There were no military targets in the centre of Vukovar to be targeted individually. It was random shelling, and the aim was to hit whatever they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, ever see airplanes in action over Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want you to deal with what you actually saw, not what you heard. Do you understand? So would you be kind enough, please, to tell us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: We were standing outside in the courtyard that day. Two planes came flying across the Danube, downstream, as it were. They came down towards Vukovar and suddenly there was a powerful explosion. Once we had taken shelter to our left, we first heard a loud bang and then we saw smoke rising not far from our own building. I realised that one of the buildings attached to the Eltz palace was on fire, the one housing the administration of the Vupik Vukovar company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you at any time on other occasions see what I will call civilian buildings being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Those were civilian buildings, the ones I've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But in addition to that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: The first shells landed near my house and the Nama department store. All the windows were shattered. Several minutes or perhaps hours later a shell landed near the Vuka high-rise and then several shells near the bridge over the Vuka. And those were the first days of shelling; that's what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In very general terms, where was what I will call the front line between JNA and Croat defenders at that time? Was that around where the shells were falling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: The lines held by Croat defenders were out in the suburbs and around Borovo Naselje. By no means did the lines coincide in the centre of town because there were no defence lines in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And this shelling or bombing of the centre of town, can you tell us the period when -- or periods when this shelling continued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: You could never know for sure when the shelling would begin or where they would strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the question that I asked you is: Over what period did this shelling occur? If we deal with August, September, November, October.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: It began when the first shells fell, and then it continued throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you were living in the centre of Vukovar at that time. You had your home there. Did you remain in that home through that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you tell the Court then where you went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: After the shelling started and we felt we were no longer safe in our apartment, the window-panes were broken, nothing could be repaired, and the shelter in my building was inadequate. It was small and it was full of water. It's -- it was a cellar. So I was forced to go to another, safer shelter. I went to the shelter across from the hospital at an apartment building where there were three floors of apartments. The ground floor was where there was a Vupik supermarket and then underneath that there was a long -- or a large shelter that was the size of the actual building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us in that account that: "We no longer felt safe." Why did you no longer feel safe in your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Because the area began to be shelled frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us when it was you actually left your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Four or five days after the first shells that I described hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like you to look, please, at an exhibit. I think it is Exhibit 156. It's the bundle of maps, and it's our map 6 which I believe has changed recently because of the pixel problem. The number is 04626622. I wonder if that can be produced, please. Now, can we blow that up slightly so that we don't need a magnifying glass, something that takes in the centre of town. Yes. Thank you very much. That looks helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we perhaps go into again private session in relation to this matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- because I'm going to ask the witness to mark where he lives.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with Dr. Bosanac and Mr. Bili Vidic. Did you see them when you were in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: When the negotiations started between the JNA and representatives of Vukovar in which Dr. Vesna Bosanac took part, as well as Marin Vidic, Bili, a few days before when they went for the first time the MUP building was set on fire with a shell, and all the staff and the police officers moved to our shelter because the shelter was big. The commander of the police at the time, Mr. Pole Stjepan, was with them as well. I saw Dr. Bosanac and Marin on two occasions when they came to speak with Mr. Pole about the course the negotiations were taking and what was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you personally have any dealings with the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: No. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal with what I will call living conditions not in the cellar but actually outside in Vukovar itself. Did you ever go into the fresh air, into Vukovar, through this period up to November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: We would all go out once the bombing of the town of Vukovar would stop. Some people would go out more frequently and some people would not go out that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was the condition of the centre of Vukovar like at that time with regard to buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I wasn't near the centre at the time, but around the building where I was, that area, everything there was demolished. The trees were bereft of leaves. Everything was knocked down. Probably the part of town where I used to live before was even more damaged than where I was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Prior to the conflict - and I'll use that word for August - were there what I will call public wells in the Vukovar city area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: There were many public wells in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And as far as you're aware, were those public wells, the location of the public wells, known to the population of Vukovar? I'm not saying all of them, but some of them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Most of the wells were privately owned in private yards, so many people who lived around that particular place or places would know about the wells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again, from your own personal knowledge, did people go to the wells to obtain water through this period from September to November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: There was no other drinking water available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how safe was it going to collect water from the wells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: People went to get water because they had to. They were thirsty. They risked their lives to bring back water for other people and for themselves, so it was not safe at all to go and get the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right to say you eventually left the shelter and went to the hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I think that it was the 15th of November when we heard that the town defence would no longer be able to hold the defence lines. I went across the road with my wife to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I -- before we move to the hospital, I just want to deal with one small area about your cellar and the people in it. Did you at any time assist any of those people in the cellar to go back to their premises to obtain items?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. I will move on then, if I may. Do you know the type of weapons that were being used or shells that were being used against Vukovar area, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: From what I was able to see, mostly it was mortar shells. They were the most frequent projectiles and they came from all sides. There were also tank projectiles, gun ammunition. All kinds of weapons were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever find shells or items that came from shells around where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: You could still find some embedded in the asphalt near the buildings where I lived or there also all over Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you able to say if these were weapons that were just specifically designed or on a target or to just injure people generally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: There was no targeting; it was just random fire and the projectiles fell wherever they fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move on to the hospital, if we may. You say you think that you went there about the 15th of November. If we try and assess numbers between the 15th and the 19th of November, how many people would you assess were in the hospital hinterland or hospital area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: When I arrived on the 15th, there weren't too many people. There were many wounded persons and the hospital staff was there. The basement was full. During those five days until the 19th, the hospital filled up and it was practically full. According to my estimate, there were about 2.500 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember the JNA arriving at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when do you think that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: That was on the 19th, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court about the arrival of the military forces, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We heard that the JNA and the rest of the forces entered Vukovar, that the defenders were giving themselves up, and sometime in the afternoon JNA soldiers came in front of the hospital and they entered the hospital. I think there was several tanks outside in front and APCs while the soldiers entered the hospital on foot?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether these were regular JNA soldiers, TO soldiers, or a specific category that we use here called Chetnik? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: The first people or soldiers whom I saw who came to the entrance hall of the hospital and were on the stairs were just regular soldiers, I think, regular soldiers of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you pause there please. Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have an objection to this quite suggestive question, making a difference between regular soldiers and soldiers allegedly called Chetniks. There were different formations in Vukovar at the time: JNA, Territorial Defence, special units, as well as Chetniks. So in future I would like my colleague, in future, when he puts such questions, not to be suggestive, not to put leading questions. That is the gist of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. It's a good point that there shouldn't be leading about specific units, but I think it is necessary to bring the witness to discuss the types of units, to indicate that a choice needs to be made, if possible, between regular JNA troops, other types of troops, and what they were. So I'm sure Mr. Moore will be able to adapt to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us the soldiers, what -- what category or type of soldiers they were who came to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: The first soldiers that I saw, as I said, well, one of them was a military officer wearing a green camouflage uniform. And there were a few soldiers with him. I don't know how many there were, and these soldiers were dressed in regular military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know who that military soldier -- that military officer was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Well, I knew after he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us his name, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: He introduced himself as Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you give a flavour, please. You say that he came. "He was wearing a green camouflage uniform." That you said "there were a few soldiers with him." Again, can you assist the Court whether they were regular, irregular, what classification, what category?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: In my opinion, these were regular soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did Major Sljivancanin speak to you? And when I say "you," I mean collectively, all of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: He introduced himself as Major Sljivancanin and said: Now you will be transported to the Velepromet warehouse where you will be separated according to what was agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he indicate what the basis of the separation was going to be at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see Major Sljivancanin having any discussion or argument with any other person who was present at the hospital that -- that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: When the military officer said this, there was some commotion. People started shoving and pushing. They couldn't bring themselves to believe that this would happen, because according to what had been agreed, buses were supposed to be on their way and people would be free to choose where they would go next. However, the agreement was not reached eventually, and Mr. Sljivancanin said people would be taken to Velepromet. After that, he turned around, went down the steps outside the hospital and spoke to two people wearing white uniforms. I did not hear their conversation, but I heard his voice telling one of those people to go back to their own country and issue orders if they like because he's in charge here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The person that he told to go back to his own country because he, Sljivancanin, was in charge, had you seen that person before or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how would you describe the tone of the way Sljivancanin dealt with that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Quite strict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And a man in a -- that he was talking to, how was he reacting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I didn't notice any reaction on his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us that Sljivancanin was with a group of -- you considered regular soldiers. At that time, how many military personnel from what I will call the JNA were around the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see how many JNA soldiers were around the hospital. I saw those people who were with Major Sljivancanin. However, when I left the hospital, outside in the courtyard there were other JNA soldiers as well as some paramilitaries who were within the hospital compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right to say that you eventually did leave the hospital and go to Velepromet. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal, please, with your transportation from the hospital to Velepromet. Have you any idea whether it was morning, afternoon, or evening when you were transported to the Velepromet area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was the method of transportation? What vehicles were you taken in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I was taken there in a military truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with one small piece of evidence that you gave about two minutes ago. You said that you saw other military personnel -- I'll just clarify for precision. One moment, please. You said that you saw paramilitaries at the hospital. Did you recognise any of those paramilitaries, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: There were many people there wearing all kinds of uniforms. I noticed several people whom I knew personally, people from Vukovar. I can perhaps give you about five or six names that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, would you be kind enough to give us those names that you believe you recognised, the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Darko Fot; Mico Dzankovic; the Susljik brothers, Cigo and his brother Susljik; Veljko Brko [phoen], I don't know his surname. I know he was a handy-man from Vukovar. Boro Kovacevic and a number of others I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How many people were actually transported with you from the hospital to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: A truckful. I'm not sure how many people that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how many trucks went to Velepromet? Were you able to see eventually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: When I came we were unloaded across the way from the warehouse in Velepromet. There was a Vupik garage there and that was where they left us. The trucks probably drove back to the hospital in order to fetch more people and bring them back to the Vupik warehouse across the way from Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But do you know how many trucks there were? Sorry, I was momentarily distracted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. There were quite many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's see if we use ten as a guide. Was it more than ten or less than ten, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I think more than ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And do you know who was driving your truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: A soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were you able to see who was driving or who were driving the other trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Soldiers, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you use the term "soldier," to which military section do they belong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I think this was the regular JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, if we just deal with your truck itself, was it just men, women, children? Can you tell the Court the make-up of the people on the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes. On my truck there were only men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then obviously the time came when you got off at Vupik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what about the other trucks? Did the people get off those trucks as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: At Vupik, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if we just deal with the light. Forget about time for a moment, let's just try dealing with lighting. Was there natural light at that time or not; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Natural light.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I didn't hear the question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm asking if you can just tell us whether there was natural light at that time when you arrived at Vupik. It helps us try and assesses time, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was still natural light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. The only reason I rose was because the witness has already answered this question, and I believe my learned friend is asking the question again, expecting the witness to perhaps change his answer. The witness has now confirmed that there was still some daylight, natural light. I think the only reason these questions are being asked is because there is the off-chance perhaps that the witness might change his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That was not the aim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I see that the witness expressly said: "I didn't not hear the question," and that is what prompted Mr. Moore to again raise the question and the question whether there was light or not. So I think that your objection is out of order. Carry on, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry. Page 23, line 8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, that's enough. Mr. Moore, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, please, with the people who got down from the truck. You've told us that -- I believe you told us that there were only men in your truck. Did you see the make-up of the people from the other trucks, whether there were men, women, or children? Can you give us a picture, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, there were women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what happened when everybody got off the trucks at Vupik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I don't know exactly if everybody got off the trucks at Vupik while I was there, but the military officials who were there started separating people on a massive scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what way did they separate the people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: As I said, there were people wearing all kinds of uniforms and insignia. They came to us, and everybody did as they saw fit. They would take as many people as they wanted. Nobody stood in their way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question that I'm asking -- you said that they were separated. Were they separated on sexual lines, ethnic lines, age lines, colour lines? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Before this time it was said that Croats should go to one side, Serbs to the other side, and everybody else to a different side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who said this, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I didn't hear exactly who.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to remember, even if it wasn't who, who was in control of the separation process?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: There was no control exercised, or at least none that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you alighted at Vupik and you were separated, was there anybody waiting for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Why would there have been? But there was a man who stepped forward from this group, a native of Vukovar, by the name of Darko Fot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what way was Darko Fot dressed, please; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to remember everything, and I can hardly remember what he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, if you can tell us, then, please, slowly what happened when you got down from the -- from the lorry. Can you tell the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: When we got off the lorry, one of my friends and I were called by Darko Fot. He sent us to one side where some of the people were who had already been separated. There were other people being taken away. After a while we were taken across the road to the Velepromet warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Who took you across to the Velepromet warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Darko Fot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did he have anybody with him when you were taken across?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: There were other soldiers there. I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how many soldiers were with Darko Fot when you were taken across?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I don't know. Quite many. They were all over the place. It's difficult to give a figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, try and see if you can assess. More than 20? Less than 20?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: More than 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were those people armed or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: All of them were, no exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what sort of arms did these people have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: To the extent that I could notice, they all had long fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you recognise or can you remember the names of people who were armed and waiting for you before going over to the Velepromet area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: In the warehouse, more specifically in the Vupik garage and in the Velepromet warehouse, there were quite a number of people from Vukovar, people I knew from Vukovar or from the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were any of those people paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: All those people belonged to a variety of paramilitary groups wearing all sorts of different uniforms and sporting all sorts of different insignia. I can't be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you remember now the names of any of those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I can, in fact, remember quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, would you be kind enough, please, to try and remember some of the names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes. Kosic, his wife Inka; her brother, we called him Kesega, their surname is Stankovic; Pero Krtinic; Dr. Maric; Cevo Zoric, his wife used to work with my wife. I remember a number of people who were there as well as those who were at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You made a statement on the 15th of May, 1992, six months after this incident at Vukovar. You've already referred to it. Now, did you check the statement to see that it was accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's go through, then, the details of how the statement was compiled. Can you tell us how you compiled the names or how you compiled the story itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: You're talking about the 1992 statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: When I came back from the hospital and from the Sremska Mitrovica camp, a police officer from the Vukovar MUP came who was staying in Zagreb at the time. This was in a neighbourhood called Spansko. We were staying in some makeshift huts there. He came to see me and to ask me about everything that had happened in Vukovar. We sat down. I told him all these names that I remembered of different people, and he took the names down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek leave from the Court for this witness to look at that document of the 15th of May, 1992, as firstly a memory refreshing document to see whether, in actual fact, any of these names are actually names that he can now remember, having been refreshed from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would the witness please be shown the document. The ERN number is 03577927, concluding at 932. The B/C/S number is 02170375.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, we do have this document, but there's one thing that I'd like to check with my learned friend. The original version of this document that is about to be shown to the witness bears the following date: The 20th of May, 1992. I see that the statement itself was taken on the 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We should be in private session for the moment if this statement is to be displayed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've reached the point where we must adjourn to allow the tapes to be rewound. As there have been redactions, there will need to be a half-hour break. We will continue after that. It would appear as long as the front page of this document doesn't go back on the screen that we can be in public session after the break, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, may we just move on, please, to this statement of May 1992. We have got to the list and the name of Darko Fot. Now, do you see that on your list? Can you just read to yourself what it says about him and can you confirm whether that's accurate or not from your memory now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The witness spoke; I certainly didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. With regard to the next name, Borislav Zuvanovic. Again, using the same procedure, the details there. Are they accurate in relation to the uniform and the long fire-arm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, they are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The next witness -- or the next name Nenad Zigic. Is that correct? Do you remember seeing him there at the Vupik Velepromet collection centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember seeing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement that he was dressed in a military uniform and it had a rank; the rank was major. Can you remember that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what sort of uniform he had and why it was you took the view he was the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: He had a dark brown uniform with the rank's insignia of a major on his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we move to the next name, Petar Velebit. Do you remember seeing him there at Vupik and then in Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Who -- he used to work with me at the former milicija, the police force, and then he went to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question is: Do you remember seeing him when you got out of your vehicle at Vupik and then subsequently went to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Marko Paic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, the suggestion is in your statement he was wearing military uniform and a long fire-arm. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Miso Rokvic, do you remember seeing him there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, he played the accordion in Vukovar. I also saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again with a fire-arm and in uniform. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have only four more other -- four more names to go through. Do you know the next name? It looks like Stevan Curnic. Is that right or not, because there's question marks at it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what is the proper name then, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: His name is Stevan Curnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And, again, the commentary in military uniform and a long fire-arm. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Stanko Vujanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: He was a taxi driver in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. But dealing with Vupik and the Velepromet area when you got out and were segregated, is this explanation, does it correspond with your memory or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Stanislav Avramovic, also known as --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My learned friend from the Prosecution asked, not for the first time, whether it is correct what it states here in this text. For example, for Stanko Vujanovic it said that he took part in guarding, denouncing, and mistreating detainees. So what is correct, only what relates to the uniform and the weapon or the whole text? I think that the witness denied saying all of these things to the person who took the statement. So I think this is something that needs to be clarified before we proceed further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the point made I think is very pertinent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I submit that a witness is entitled to look at a document where the indicia for reliability suggests that he is the source of the documentation. If a witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the point is: What is it is he saying to be correct? There have been clear indications that not everything recorded are his words. The only express things that he's indicated is that he saw the person in uniform carrying a fire-arm. There is much more recorded, which is quite different from any of his evidence to date. If you want any specific notice to be taken of that, it will need to be explored properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the way I propose to do it, and I hope it meets the agreement of the Defence, is for the witness to read the document, ask whether in actual fact he remembers the person as being there from his present recollection, and whether the explanation given in the document accords with his present recollection. And that is all I would wish to establish at this time. It may well be that I would want to deal with these individuals later on in his evidence, and I hope that that would be an appropriate way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For my part I want it to be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- clear that he agrees with everything that is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or only part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That seems to be the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly, I will do that. Does my learned friend wish me to go back to the name of Zigic as a starting point, which is only two names back, and that is really -- is fairly close to where we resumed. I'm quite happy to resume at a particular name if there's any concern about an individual. I see my learned friend nodding yes, and I will do it that way with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, I want you to go back, please, to the name of Nenad Zigic. There is written beside his name an explanation or an account of what he was supposed to have done. Can you read that out, please, and tell us whether you agree if that is accurate or not. Now, can you read it out, please, and tell the Court whether it is accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: "I saw Nenad Zigic in a uniform with the ranks of major. The rest I did not see."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we look at Petar Velebit. Now, you have a commentary. Can we do the same again, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Once again, I say that I saw him in uniform and armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is another part that relates to another aspect about defenders and civilians. Is that accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I really don't know that. I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us move then to Marko Paic. Again, there is an explanation. Firstly, did you see Marko Paic at Vupik and Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was also in uniform and armed, but as for the rest I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Miso Rokvic, did you see him at Vupik Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: In a uniform and with weapons, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we go back to Stevan Curnic. You've told us you saw him. What about the other entry, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: The same, in a uniform with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Stanko Vujanovic you've told us you saw. Please read what is said there for him and confirm whether that is accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I repeat, once again, that I saw him in a uniform with a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember anything else about Vujanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Not right now, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Stanislav Avramovic, did you see him at Vupik Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes. He also was wearing a uniform and had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the final one, are you able to assist with that name or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: He was a driver. He worked at the same company that I did. He also wore a uniform and had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just listen then to the following question. You have given those names to the Court as being people who met you at Vupik. What were they doing after that; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I don't know what they did after that. I wasn't able to be at every place where they happened to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we then deal, please, at -- when you've arrived at Vupik and you've told us about the separation. You've already explained that. What then happened to your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: During the transfer from Vupik to Velepromet, we were taken to a wall which is on the left side next to the Velepromet entrance. More people were being brought in from all directions. After a certain amount of time, not too long afterwards, I was summoned by Mico Dzankovic, a former waiter in Vukovar from a group, and he told me to stand a little bit to the side. A young man stood next to me - I knew him from Ilok - who was a police officer in Vukovar at the time. His name was Miroslav Blaskovic. Miro Dzankovic took him out from that group also and told him to stand next to me next to that wall. After a certain amount of time he cursed him, cursed his mother, and then he hit him on the face with the barrel of his rifle. Blood started to show on his face, and then they took him off somewhere, and I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want you, please, to look at a document. The number is 04672780, and I believe -- well, the Defence will have copies of that. Could that be put on the screen, please. Now, I think it's right to say that when you came to The Hague on this occasion that you brought this document with you. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the document itself represents the Vupik-Velepromet area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I wonder if it's possible for the document to be enlarged? It's rather difficult on my screen to see it. I think it can't be minimised to an appropriate size.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal with the document itself. At the top of the page we have got an arrow pointing to Negoslavci. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And we have got at the bottom an arrow pointing to Vukovar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in between we have got a road clearly running in a north-south direction between Negoslavci and Vukovar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I just deal with a general understanding and then we'll move on to specifics. But did you actually compile the buildings themselves? So I'm not talking about the arrow marks; I'm talking about the buildings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you just tell the Court how this document was created initially? Just in very simple terms, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: It was done for me by a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long ago was it done for you, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: About six months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, we have got arrows clearly drawn coming from the left-hand side and then going into what seems to be the Velepromet area. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let us just look to the left-hand side of the page, what I will call 9.00. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, what is that area on the left-hand side of the page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: This is the Vupik warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when you talk about the Vupik warehouse, is that the warehouse area where you were offloaded from the lorries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you explain to us then exactly what the arrows represent.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: This is the route along which I was taken to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You're talking about the arrows. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can you with your magic pencil and the electronic screen - I don't know if it's possible or not - actually mark out the route that you actually took, not the route of others, the route that you took.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to stop there for a moment, please. Now, your marking shows you're coming in from the Vupik area, across the road, into Velepromet, and then you seem to go to a location and then leave that location. Now, what happened? Can you explain to the Court exactly what this diagram represents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: The whole thing, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, if you just tell us what it is you have drawn and explain to us slowly what happened and where. So take your time and tell us as thoroughly as you wish.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: This is the Vupik warehouse. I was offloaded here and so were they. This is where the group was formed and we were taken behind this wall for the first time, roughly speaking. The next time I was taken away it was to this spot that I've just marked. The third time around I was taken to this spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that, but we just need to mark out the spots that you're referring to. So let's use the magic pen again. Can you tell us, using the pen, where it is that you go and where you stop. And tell us then what happens there and then move on again. Would you do that? And mark on the diagram, please, where you stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: The first time around we stopped right here near the casino on our way from Vupik to Velepromet. From that group of people, Mico Dzankovic took me to one side and two other people, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So every time that you refer to stopping, mark it with a -- let us say, an X or an A. It matters not. So you stop there. Who takes you there, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Mico Dzankovic called me to one side and led me there with a number of other people. As I have already said, he --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who is Mico Dzankovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who is Mico Dzankovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Mico Dzankovic was a waiter before the war in Vukovar. He is from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was Mico Dzankovic doing that evening with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: He just took me to one side and put me in a different group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when he put you into the different group, how many did he put you -- how many were in that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: About seven or eight persons, ten at most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so where was the group? Where did it -- where was it placed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: The group was right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was happening at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: You mean happening to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you can tell us what was happening to you and perhaps tell us what was happening to others. You see, I can't tell you what to say; you've got to tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Fine. People were still being separated left and right on a massive scale. This was done in an arbitrary fashion. Mico Dzankovic was the one who separated me and a couple of other people from the rest, left us there with about ten other people. They were still bringing other people to that group. After a while, Boro Zuvanovic came for the third time, called my name out, and told me to leave the group, together with another man whose name I believe was Jurica. When he started leading us toward the buildings over there I asked him: Boro, where are you taking us? And he said: (redacted), just keep your mouth shut. There's going to be quite a mess here. I'm taking you somewhere safe. And then we headed towards this spot I've marked here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say you headed towards this spot here, can you put a C, a letter C at this spot, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can we mark the other spots A and B, obviously running in sequence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So with regard to A, what happened at A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: We were brought here from Vupik near the wall to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then at B?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: The spot marked as B. When Mico Dzankovic took me to one side, I described what happened between Mico Dzankovic and the police officer Boro Draskovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What was the atmosphere like in Velepromet at that time when you came in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: It's very difficult to describe it verbally. There was panic and fear in the air. Sounds of shooting could be heard from the moment I arrived throughout. This shooting -- what should I call it? There was shooting all over the place. There was celebratory fire, people firing into the air, and other people firing. I didn't know why they were firing. You could hear screams, women screaming for the most part, Bring back my this or my that, because they were taking people away and women were crying. It was a scene of utter chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with the movement from B to C on your diagram. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us then what occurred when you were moving from B to C?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: When leaving B -- or rather, when Boro Zuvanovic called me, it was next to this building, I'm not sure what it is now, a small building, I saw a man who passed in front of us, Mirko, also known as Capalo. He was walking ahead of us holding a crooked knife in his hand, a knife with a crooked tip, with blood dripping from it. In his other hand he was carrying a human head. I'm 90 per cent certain that what I saw was a human head. He passed in front of us and never looked back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you mark a letter D if it's possible where it was you saw this man called Capalo with the knife and the head. If you can't do it, just tell us whether it was in an open area or an enclosed area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: It was in an open area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you saw this man Capalo with the knife and what you felt sure was a head in his other hand, what did you feel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I was horrified. I didn't have time to think about anything at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I'm just watching the time moving by on this sketch that has been marked --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If we don't tender it soon, we may lose the marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I was aware of that. I was hoping to get to the destination. Can I just ask this question of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, if you think this -- you're getting somewhere shortly, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will. Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And D, what was D on your map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: D.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: C, I was one ahead. I'm sorry about that. C.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: C marks the spot where that small building was in front of which I was brought. Me and that other person called Jurica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps if we take a photograph of that now and tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Prior to actually going to that small room, did you see within the Velepromet area where you were walking through, did you see anyone in military uniform or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: They were all over the place. There were people all over the place, but less people than I saw around the admin building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal then, please, with the small room that you went to. Can you describe it for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: It's a very small room with a slanting roof, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that -- did you go into the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: The two of us were brought just outside that small room. A man was standing there wearing camouflage uniform, very tall, with long hair and a beard. Just in front of him there was a table. This man who was leading us, Boro, said to him Topola: These two are mine, don't let anyone get near them or touch them. And he answered: No problem there, Boro. Boro left, went somewhere, and then Topola ordered me to place a bag that I was holding on a heap of other bags that were lying there. I was wearing a jeans jacket, somewhat long, with fur lining. He told me to take it off and place that, too, on top of that heap. We did as we were told. After that he told me to hand over my documents. I extracted all the documents from my wallet and in fact handed over the entire wallet. There was some money; he took the money and placed the money on the table in front of him and laid the documents down under the table. I saw that there were other documents under the table, too, just like mine. I turned around. I was wearing a small and flimsy black jacket, and he said: Take that off, too, and put it on top of that heap. I did that, and I was left in a -- wearing a T-shirt, and he ordered the other man who was with me to do the same thing. Since it was very cold and we were freezing, I asked if I could have my leather jacket back as well as my documents. And he replied: You won't be needing these anymore. After some time he opened the door and told us to get in. I was the first to get into the building, and he kicked Jurica on his way in. We were now inside the building, and the door slammed shut behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal, if we can, please, with what you found inside the building after you had been placed inside it. Were there any other people in there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Two or three candles were burning. I can't remember exactly. The small building was packed with people who were there already when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I know it's very difficult to estimate numbers, but can you give the Court an idea of numbers? More or less than 50?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I think just over 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was the atmosphere like in that particular building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: When I came in there was a deadly silence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And do you know what that room or building was subsequently titled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Some called it the death cell. Some called it the carpenter's room, which is what it was, what it was used for, as part of the Velepromet company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you were in the room you described it as being silent. Did you hear any noises outside that caught your attention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: All we could hear while we were inside was sounds of firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how close was the firing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: One couldn't really discern or distinguish the exact spot that sounds of firing were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But did there come a time when there was firing right beside the building itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: After I came in -- well, after a certain time, it's difficult to say exactly, there was firing just outside the door of that building, and people were yelling things like: He's getting away. He's getting away. Catch him, quickly. After a while the door opened and a young man was thrown or pushed into the building. Both his legs were bleeding. I recognised him. I know this young man well. His name was Dragan Lucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have described -- you have described that his legs were bleeding. Did you see what had caused the injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: There was a doctor who wanted to dress his wounds, but he had nothing to dress them with. I think his name was Josip Nadas. He bent down over him, and he says he has gun-shot wounds to both his knees and his ankles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you do anything to try and help Dragan Lucic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: There was nothing I could do at this point in time. Dr. Nadas was trying to help. I gave him my own shirt to use to try to help the young man's life and stop the bleeding; however, we failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you speak to anybody outside the room about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: We realised that he was bleeding profusely and that there was nothing we could do. I knocked on the door of that other room, and then this soldier named Topola came in and asked what was going on. And I said: There is a man, he's dying, can we do anything to save him? After a while, two persons came in and took Dragan away from the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Dragan -- was Dragan ever brought back to the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Dragan was brought back, and there were bandages on his legs. However, there was still some bleeding and Dr. Nadas did whatever he could to stop that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's continue with the room. Did any other people come into that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: After Dragan was brought there, the door opened and a young man emerged in the door. He had long blond hair and a beard. He held a bottle of some alcohol in one hand and an automatic rifle in the other. He stood there in the doorway saying: At about 9.00, or half past 9.00 latest, you'll all be taken to be executed. He lingered there for a minute or two and then left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, after he left, can you then again slowly tell us what then happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Fear and panic descended upon us. We felt certain that we would die. We kept looking at one another, but nobody said anything. Soon after, the door opened again and a man in uniform emerged. I think he had the rank of major. He had two soldiers on each side accompanying him. At first we thought this was the firing-squad and they were about to shoot us. However, this turned out to be something altogether different, to our great fortune. This man came in and said: People, stand up, all of you. They had been calling us Ustashas all the while, but this man was the first not to use the term. He said: People, stand up. Walk in twos, hold each other's hands, don't look left or right, just go out. There's a bus waiting for you there. Get on the bus without looking left or right. None of us could believe this at first. I was particularly diffident by the way things went, that things had taken a totally different turn now. We grabbed each other's hands. There was a man standing next to me, Mirko Bridovic, he was an inspector in Vukovar, a sanitation inspector. We slowly walked towards the bus, heads down, the bus waiting for us outside. The military officer expressly ordered his people: Turn around, no one is to come even close. If anyone comes close, shoot them. It was at this point in time that it dawned on me that we were now saved. We got on to the bus and so did the officer. He spoke to the driver who was also in uniform. He said: Just drive on, park somewhere along the road to Negoslavci, and pull over right behind that Pinzgauer. He also told two soldiers to guard the doors, one each. He said: No one is to get on this bus but me. And the soldiers complied with this. We set out. We left the Velepromet compound, and - I'm sorry - parked behind this Pinzgauer that was parked there facing Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, are you all right or would you need a break?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Everything's all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say then that you were taken away, is that right, to safety?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with one or two areas in relation to your knowledge of Vukovar and the people in Vukovar. Do you know the Dosen family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I know the Dosen family; most people in Vukovar do. His mother lived in my building in the centre, where I was living, on the first floor, Ms. Marija Dosen. There were three Dosen brothers, Tadija, Martin, and Ivica. They had two sisters. We used to call one Seka and the other one we called Crna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How would you describe the Dosen family before, let us say, the summer of 1991? Were they a politically active family or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: They were all employed. The eldest, Tadija, worked at the Borovo company as a labourer. The second one is Martin; he worked in the agricultural combine, and then later he became a professional fisherman. The third brother, Ivica, worked occasionally. He wasn't permanently employed. From what I know, they were not really interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with them, though, whether you knew -- whether you know whether they were defenders of Vukovar or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does that relate to all three brothers or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: I know about the oldest and the youngest. I'm not sure about the middle one, but I think that he was part of the defence, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And as far as you're aware, how well-known as defenders were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: They didn't behave as people who wanted to be especially known. They just behaved like any other of the defenders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's right to say that you were shown a list of people - the Court will know it as the annex to the indictment - a list of people who are described as victims at Ovcara. Do you remember seeing that document? I'll just hold it up so you can see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, I remember seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive me for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm told that it's saved as 00 Ovcara in e-court. I've got it now showing, but there are certain markings that are not terribly easy to see. Can we blow it up the first page and then we'll move through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've told my learned friends, so that there's no misunderstanding, some of the marks here are actually mine from my indictment, but I wanted for my own understanding to know what this witness thought were people who were seen at the hospital when he was there. So there are marks on it, but I will just deal with the Hs and I will clarify that they are his.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, can you just look at this document for a moment. I think it's right to say that you were asked to look at this list of people and mark with the letter H those that you remember seeing at the hospital. Is that right or not? Can you just answer, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when we look at this first page, and we'll move on, I think it's right to say if we scan down the page, if that's possible to do it slowly, please, that with the markings of H those are your markings of people you believed to have seen at the hospital when you were there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I just clarify with the witness, there is at the name of Blaskovic, Miroslav, a mark of V/not hospital. That is not your marking. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: All I wrote was the letter V.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But can we just deal with the Hs for a moment. So the Hs are yours. That's right, I think?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, let's look at this page, and we've got Blaskovic, Miroslav. There is a V opposite that. Is that your V or not, standing for Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, that is my V.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I am quite happy to go through to the next page, please, if that's possible. Can that be done? Again, you have got Hs running down opposite various names. Again, same format. Is that your H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what does the H stand for here on this page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: It means that I saw those people at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Moving over to the next page, please. Thank you very much. Does the same apply to those Hs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we look at the initial M and there is a V, Marijanovic. Do you see that, that V there? Can the registry please move on to the initial M because it does go alphabetically. The next page, please. The next page, please. Now, do you see the -- we've got Hs, two Hs and a V. Is that your V, is that your marking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Hs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we move on then two more pages with the first name as Magdic at the very top. I see I've got a duplication here. That's a duplication. And with regard to the rest of the indictment, if we go to the initial J -- sorry, the initial T for Tomasic. Have we got that? Can we turn to the next page, please. And again there are four Hs. Did you mark those four Hs as people that you saw at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Could you please scroll the page down. I did write that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would seek to make that an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, one of the names I did not refer you to was your son. And I don't want to mention his name or draw attention to it in open court. But I think it's right to say that your son's name is specified on that list of victims of Ovcara. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-007
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
